abstract: Federal Reserve economists Leland Crane and Paul Soto compile evidence on AI's impact on software developer employment, focusing on coding-intensive occupations as a leading indicator of broader labor market disruption. Using O*NET data linked to Current Population Survey (CPS) employment counts, the authors find that aggregate employment growth of coders has decelerated sharply since the introduction of ChatGPT in November 2022. After controlling for industry-level shocks using a novel between-industry/within-industry decomposition, they find robust evidence that annual coder employment growth is approximately 3 percentage points lower than it was pre-ChatGPT. The deceleration is not attributable to exposure of coders to slowing industries, suggesting an occupation-specific shock. The authors note that coding is one of the most LLM-exposed tasks, and that if generative AI is to substantially affect the labor market, coding-intensive occupations are where effects should appear first. They also find about 40% of coders work in computer systems design and related services (NAICS 5415), not in the information sector (NAICS 51) often used to proxy the tech industry.
keyFindings: Annual coder employment growth is approximately 3 percentage points lower post-ChatGPT than pre-ChatGPT, after controlling for industry-level shocks, suggesting an occupation-specific AI effect.

The employment deceleration is not attributable to coders being concentrated in slowing industries — the within-industry/between-industry decomposition attributes a substantial fraction to occupation-specific factors.
About 40% of coders work in computer systems design (NAICS 5415), not the information sector (NAICS 51) commonly used to proxy the tech industry, complicating sector-based analyses of AI impact.
Coder employment has continued to grow in recent years but much more slowly than pre-2022 trends, consistent with AI tools absorbing some demand for human coding labor.
Different generative AI exposure measures (Eloundou et al. 2024 vs. Handa et al. 2025) show notable disagreement for many occupations, though both agree coders are among the most highly exposed.
methodology: Event study design treating the introduction of ChatGPT (November 2022) as the treatment event. Uses O*NET data to identify coding-intensive occupations, linked to CPS for monthly employment tracking. Develops a novel industry-level control variable based on within-industry/between-industry decomposition of occupational employment growth to distinguish industry-level from occupation-specific shocks. Validates the control variable using historical examples of known occupation-specific and industry-level shocks. Published March 2026 as a FEDS working paper.
qualifiers: The authors acknowledge they cannot control for AI's effects on aggregate labor demand or prices, and that occupational task mix may be changing in ways that overstate effects on coders as a skill group. The analysis cannot capture general equilibrium effects. The short post-treatment window (approximately 3 years) limits statistical power and may conflate transitional adjustment with permanent structural change. CPS data are survey-based and subject to sampling error for occupation-level estimates. The occupation-specific shock interpretation assumes AI, but other factors could contribute.
